That absence strongly suggests IMDSv1 is enabled / not enforced — IMDSv2 would require a token obtained via PUT and passed as the X-aws-ec2-metadata-token header. (Caveat: confirm your log pipeline actually captures PUTs before concluding it's v1.)
Three plausible explanations, in order of "boring" to "bad":

Benign misconfiguration — invoice-api uses the AWS SDK, IRSA/Pod Identity isn't set up, so the SDK's credential chain falls back to node IMDS on every credential refresh. This produces these exact lines, repeatedly, forever.
SSRF — a request-forgery flaw in the invoice API let an external caller coerce the pod into fetching the metadata URL.
Post-compromise — an attacker with code execution in the container is harvesting credentials (MITRE ATT&CK T1552.005, Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata API).

Discriminators to settle which one it is: does invoice-api use IRSA (if yes, it should never need node IMDS — escalate)? Is there a correlated inbound request in the app logs around 04:12:33 carrying a URL/host parameter pointing at 169.254.169.254 (→ SSRF)? Is the access periodic and identical (→ SDK refresh) or one-off/bursty (→ more suspicious)? And most decisively — were the resulting credentials used from anywhere unexpected (sections 3 below)?
2. What may be exposed
The credential endpoint returns temporary STS credentials for the node role, shaped like:
json{
  "Code": "Success",
  "Type": "AWS-HMAC",
  "AccessKeyId": "ASIA...",
  "SecretAccessKey": "...",
  "Token": "...",
  "Expiration": "2026-05-21T10:12:00Z"
}
The ASIA prefix confirms these are temporary credentials. They carry whatever the app-role node instance role is permitted to do. On a typical EKS node that's at least ECR pull, the CNI policy, and the worker-node policy — but the real risk is over-permissioning, which is extremely common (S3 access, sts:AssumeRole into other roles, Secrets Manager, etc.). Audit the role's attached and inline policies to know the true blast radius.
Critically for containment: these credentials remain valid until their Expiration, from anywhere, even after you fix the pod. Exfiltrated creds don't care that the instance later rotated them.
Beyond credentials, the same IMDS exposure means an attacker could also read other paths: instance-id, region/AZ, VPC/subnet and security-group info, the AMI ID, SSH public keys, and — the one that bites people — **/latest/user-data**, which frequently contains bootstrap scripts, tokens, or secrets. Check whether your user-data holds anything sensitive.
3. Cloud audit logs to review for subsequent use
This is where you determine malicious vs. benign. Pivot on the AccessKeyId.
GuardDuty is the highest-signal source and is purpose-built for this. Look for UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS and ...InstanceCredentialExfiltration.InsideAWS — these fire when instance-role credentials are used from an IP/account that isn't the instance itself. If GuardDuty is enabled and silent, that's meaningfully reassuring; if it fired, treat as confirmed exfiltration.
CloudTrail is the system of record. First get the ASIA key id from the credentials, then run (CloudWatch Logs Insights, if CloudTrail → CloudWatch):
sqlfields @timestamp, eventName, eventSource, sourceIPAddress, awsRegion,
       userIdentity.arn, userIdentity.accessKeyId, errorCode, userAgent
| filter userIdentity.accessKeyId = "ASIA_THE_KEY_FROM_THE_CRED_RESPONSE"
| sort @timestamp asc
To catch external use of the role generally (adjust CIDRs to your VPC ranges; note legitimate service calls show sourceIPAddress like ec2.amazonaws.com):
sqlfields @timestamp, eventName, eventSource, sourceIPAddress, userIdentity.arn
| filter userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName = "app-role"
| filter (sourceIPAddress not like /^10\./
          and sourceIPAddress not like /^172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\./
          and sourceIPAddress not like /^192\.168\./
          and sourceIPAddress not like /amazonaws\.com$/)
| sort @timestamp asc
Note a subtlety: exfiltrated creds appear in CloudTrail under the same assumed-role session name as legitimate use (the session name is the instance id, baked into the credential). So you distinguish good from bad by sourceIPAddress, userAgent, and the nature of the calls — not by session name.
What to hunt for in those results: reconnaissance (Describe*/List*/Get* bursts), persistence (CreateUser, CreateAccessKey, AttachUserPolicy, PutUserPolicy, CreateRole), privilege/lateral movement (AssumeRole into other roles), data access (s3:GetObject on sensitive buckets, secretsmanager:GetSecretValue), and defense evasion (StopLogging, DeleteTrail, GuardDuty DeleteDetector). Also pull VPC Flow Logs for the pod's node to confirm the metadata access and spot any large outbound transfers (exfiltration), and check CloudTrail data events for S3/Lambda if enabled.
4. Containment
Order matters: preserve evidence, then revoke, then isolate, then root-cause.
The single most important action for stolen instance creds is to revoke active sessions on the role, since you can't individually expire already-issued temporary credentials. In the IAM console, the role's "Revoke active sessions" button attaches an inline deny that invalidates every session issued before "now":
json{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Deny",
    "Action": ["*"],
    "Resource": ["*"],
    "Condition": { "DateLessThan": { "aws:TokenIssueTime": "2026-05-21T05:00:00Z" } }
  }]
}
This immediately kills any exfiltrated credentials regardless of their Expiration. (Legitimate workloads on the node will re-request fresh creds, which is fine — though it's a sign you should move them to IRSA.)
Then: snapshot the node's EBS volume and capture the pod (container filesystem / process list) before you destroy anything if you intend to do forensics; cordon and drain the node, and delete or network-isolate the invoice-api-7f9d pod; rotate any secrets the role could reach and anything that lived in user-data; and review CloudTrail (section 3) for attacker-created persistence (new IAM users/keys/roles, unexpected Lambdas) and roll those back. Finally, fix the entry vector — patch the SSRF in invoice-api or remediate the compromise — before redeploying, or you'll just get re-owned.
5. Hardening controls for metadata access
Layered, from most to least impactful for this scenario:
Give pods their own scoped identity via IRSA or EKS Pod Identity, so application pods never need node IMDS. This is the structural fix — once pods have their own credentials, you can block node IMDS for them entirely without breaking anything.
Block pod access to IMDS at the network layer. A NetworkPolicy denying egress to the link-local address:
yamlapiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-imds-egress
  namespace: invoicing
spec:
  podSelector: {}            # all pods in the namespace
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
            except:
              - 169.254.169.254/32
(Requires a CNI that enforces egress policy, e.g. Calico/Cilium; the AWS VPC CNI needs the Network Policy add-on enabled.)
Enforce IMDSv2 and clamp the hop limit on the node launch template / instances:
bashaws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options \
  --instance-id i-xxxx \
  --http-tokens required \
  --http-put-response-hop-limit 1 \
  --http-endpoint enabled
http-tokens=required defeats most SSRF (the attacker can't do the required PUT + header through a GET-only forgery). hop-limit=1 is the EKS-specific lever: the extra network hop out of a pod's namespace decrements the response TTL below 1, so the node itself can still reach IMDS but pods cannot. Verify against your CNI — a few host-networking setups need 2, which is why IRSA + NetworkPolicy is the more robust combination.
Least-privilege the node role — strip it to the EKS managed policies and nothing application-specific. Application permissions belong on per-workload IRSA roles, not the shared node role.
Advanced: constrain where node-role credentials can be used with an SCP using aws:SourceVpc / aws:VpcSourceIp conditions, so even leaked node creds are denied when called from outside your VPCs. Test this carefully in a non-prod OU first — service-initiated calls and cross-service flows can trip overly broad conditions.
6. Detection logic for future attempts
Detect at three layers.
Host / container (Falco) — catches the access at the source regardless of IMDS version:
yaml- rule: Contact Cloud Metadata Service From Container
  desc: >
    Container reached the cloud instance metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254).
    Common credential-theft vector via SSRF or post-compromise (T1552.005).
  condition: >
    outbound and container and fd.sip = "169.254.169.254"
    and not k8s.pod.name in (imds_allowlisted_pods)
  output: >
    Container contacted instance metadata service
    (command=%proc.cmdline pid=%proc.pid connection=%fd.name
     image=%container.image.repository pod=%k8s.pod.name ns=%k8s.ns.name)
  priority: WARNING
  tags: [network, mitre_credential_access, T1552.005]
Maintain imds_allowlisted_pods for any workload that legitimately needs node IMDS (ideally empty once you're on IRSA).
Network (VPC Flow Logs / eBPF) — alert on any non-allowlisted pod with egress flows to 169.254.169.254, which is cheap and version-agnostic. If you have a service mesh or Cilium with HTTP visibility, alert specifically on the …/iam/security-credentials/ path.
Control plane (CloudTrail anomaly) — the highest-fidelity confirmation: node-role credentials used from a source IP outside your VPC CIDRs. Expressed as a Sigma rule for your SIEM:
yamltitle: AWS Instance Role Credentials Used From Unexpected Source
logsource:
  product: aws
  service: cloudtrail
detection:
  selection:
    userIdentity.type: AssumedRole
    userIdentity.sessionContext.sessionIssuer.userName: 'app-role'
  filter_internal:
    sourceIPAddress|startswith:
      - '10.'
      - '172.16.'    # extend to your full RFC1918 / VPC ranges
      - '192.168.'
  filter_services:
    sourceIPAddress|endswith: '.amazonaws.com'
  condition: selection and not (filter_internal or filter_services)
level: high
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1552.005
And make sure GuardDuty is enabled org-wide with findings routed to your SIEM/on-call — its InstanceCredentialExfiltration detectors are essentially a managed version of the CloudTrail rule above and will often beat your custom logic to the alert.

If it's useful, I can bundle the Falco rule, NetworkPolicy, Sigma rule, the IAM revoke policy, and the CloudTrail queries into ready-to-apply files. I'd also suggest confirming the IRSA question first — whether invoice-api is supposed to reach node IMDS is the fastest way to know if you're looking at a misconfiguration or an intrusion.

response_text:
Cloud metadata services sit at the link-local address 169.254.169.254 (part of the RFC 3927 169.254.0.0/16 range) and are reachable from any workload running on the instance. The cloud platform implicitly trusts requests originating from the instance itself, so by default there's no authentication between the workload and the metadata endpoint. That trust model is the root of most of the risk below.
1. What data may be exposed
The metadata service returns information about the instance and, critically, often returns credentials:

Instance and network details: instance ID, type, image ID, region/zone, account/project ID, private and public IPs, MAC address, subnet and security group info. Useful for reconnaissance but not directly dangerous.
User data / startup scripts: the bootstrap scripts passed at launch (e.g., AWS /latest/user-data). These frequently contain hardcoded secrets, API keys, database passwords, or configuration that shouldn't be readable by an arbitrary process.
Identity credentials — the high-value target:

AWS: /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role> returns temporary AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and Token.
GCP: /computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/token returns an OAuth2 access token (requires a Metadata-Flavor: Google header).
Azure: /metadata/identity/oauth2/token issues a managed-identity token (requires a Metadata: true header).


SSH keys and custom metadata/tags in some configurations.

2. Why metadata credentials are sensitive
These credentials are the workload's cloud identity. Whoever holds them can call cloud APIs with whatever the instance's role or service account is permitted to do — and roles are very commonly over-provisioned. That enables enumeration (GetCallerIdentity, ListBuckets, Describe*), data access, lateral movement, and sometimes privilege escalation if the role can modify IAM. They're temporary, but valid for a window (often hours) and re-fetchable as long as the endpoint is reachable.
The canonical example is the 2019 Capital One breach: a server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw was used to reach the metadata service, retrieve credentials for an over-privileged role, and exfiltrate roughly 100M+ records from S3. SSRF-to-metadata is the dominant exploitation pattern — an attacker who can coerce a vulnerable app into making a request to 169.254.169.254 doesn't need code execution to steal the identity.
3. How defenders detect access
The challenge is that legitimate access is constant (cloud agents and SDKs refresh credentials routinely), so detection is about anomalous access, not access per se:

Process context (host-based): runtime tools like Falco, or EDR with eBPF, can flag connections to the metadata IP from processes that have no business making them — e.g., an nginx, php, or java web process hitting the IAM credentials path rather than the cloud agent doing so.
Path specificity: access to the credentials path or user-data is far higher signal than generic instance metadata.
Application/WAF layer: WAF rules can catch SSRF attempts where a request parameter contains a link-local or private IP, or the literal metadata path.
Credential-use correlation: the strongest signal is catching the stolen credential being used from somewhere it shouldn't be. AWS GuardDuty's UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration finding fires when credentials minted for an EC2 instance are used from an external IP or a different account — it catches exfiltration regardless of how the creds were obtained.

4. Hardening controls

Session-based metadata (AWS IMDSv2): requires a PUT to obtain a token, then the token in a header on subsequent requests. Typical SSRF (GET-only, no custom headers) can't complete this handshake, so enforcing HttpTokens: required blocks most SSRF-based theft. Set the hop limit to 1 so the response can't traverse a NAT, proxy, or container boundary — this also prevents containers from reaching the host's IMDS.
Header requirements (GCP/Azure): the mandatory Metadata-Flavor: Google / Metadata: true headers already defeat naive SSRF. On GCP, disable legacy endpoints (disable-legacy-endpoints) that didn't enforce the header.
Network blocking: deny egress to 169.254.169.254 for workloads that don't need metadata (iptables, Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, cloud egress rules). Disable the endpoint entirely (HttpEndpoint: disabled) where it's unused.
Least-privilege roles: the single most important damage-capping control. If credentials leak, minimal permissions limit the blast radius.
Workload identity federation: on Kubernetes, prefer EKS IRSA / GKE Workload Identity / Azure Workload Identity, which issue scoped, per-workload credentials via projected tokens and OIDC — letting you block node IMDS for pods entirely instead of relying on it. (This supersedes older proxy approaches like kube2iam/kiam.)
App-layer SSRF defense: validate and allowlist outbound URLs; reject requests targeting link-local and private ranges.

5. How cloud audit logs reveal misuse
An important nuance first: the metadata request itself is generally not in cloud audit logs. It's a local link-local request handled by the hypervisor, not an API call, so CloudTrail/Cloud Audit Logs won't show "instance queried IMDS." Detecting the actual fetch requires the host/network telemetry in point 3. What the audit logs capture is the downstream misuse of the stolen credentials:

AWS CloudTrail: every API call made with the credentials appears with the assumed-role session in userIdentity and a sourceIPAddress. For instance-profile credentials, the session name in the ARN typically embeds the instance ID (.../RoleName/i-1234567890abcdef0), so you can check whether the call's source IP matches that instance's real IP. A mismatch — or a burst of recon calls (GetCallerIdentity, ListBuckets, Describe*) shortly after deploy — strongly suggests exfiltrated creds.
GCP Cloud Audit Logs (Admin Activity / Data Access) and Azure Activity + sign-in logs play the same role for service accounts and managed identities.
Threat-detection services (GuardDuty and equivalents) fuse these logs with network/DNS data to raise the exfiltration findings automatically.

The practical hunt is: when was a credential first used, from what IP/geolocation, and is the activity consistent with the workload's normal behavior — anything from outside your cloud's known IP ranges, or any unexpected enumeration/privilege activity, warrants investigation.
If it's useful, I'm happy to map the typical SSRF→metadata→API-misuse chain as a diagram, or go deeper on detection rules (e.g., concrete Falco/GuardDuty logic) for whichever cloud you're working in.

This policy is effectively near-admin through indirection. It never says iam:* or *:*, but the combination of iam:PassRole on * with a compute service that can assume roles means it can very likely escalate to whatever the most privileged role in the account is. Here's the full breakdown against your six asks.
1. Risk assessment
Critical. Three problems compound:

iam:PassRole on Resource: * with no iam:PassedToService condition — this is the keystone. PassRole does nothing alone, but it's the permission that lets a principal hand any role to an AWS service. Unscoped, it means "pass any role, including admin, to anything."
s3:* on * — full read/write/delete/configure on every bucket in the account. Always-live, no escalation required to cause major damage.
ec2:RunInstances + lambda:CreateFunction on * — the compute services that turn PassRole into code execution under a borrowed role.

Individually each is over-broad. Together, PassRole + RunInstances is a recognized direct path to account takeover.
2. Privilege-escalation paths (defender's view)
Path A — PassRole + RunInstances (primary, often self-contained).
An attacker launches an EC2 instance with an instance profile for a more-privileged role, then reads that role's temporary credentials from the instance metadata service (http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role>, token-gated under IMDSv2 but readable from on the box). They now hold that role's credentials. If it's an admin/iam:* role, that's full takeover.
Important nuance for accuracy: this is fully self-contained only if a privileged role already has an instance profile. If not, the attacker also needs iam:CreateInstanceProfile / iam:AddRoleToInstanceProfile, which this policy does not grant. In practice most accounts have at least one privileged role with an existing instance profile (anything that's ever run on a managed EC2 fleet), so treat this as live.
Path B — PassRole + CreateFunction (latent, needs a trigger).
Create a Lambda with a privileged execution role; the function code then acts as that role (exfil its creds or perform admin actions). With only lambda:CreateFunction granted here, the attacker still needs an invoke/trigger primitive — lambda:InvokeFunction, CreateEventSourceMapping, CreateFunctionUrlConfig, or AddPermission — none of which are in this excerpt. So this path is not complete from this policy alone, but it becomes live the instant any invoke or event-source capability appears elsewhere on this principal. Flag it as a primed escalation primitive.
Path C — S3-assisted escalation/lateral movement.
s3:* is a data-plane path to credentials and code:

Terraform state, CI/CD artifacts, and app config in S3 routinely contain plaintext secrets, DB passwords, and sometimes long-lived access keys. Reading those escalates laterally.
If Lambda deployment packages or EC2 user-data/bootstrap scripts live in writable buckets, tampering with them injects code into whatever privileged role runs them (supply-chain-style).
s3:* includes PutBucketPolicy/PutBucketAcl/DeleteObject, enabling public exposure, and disabling/deleting CloudTrail log objects — defense evasion that supports the rest.

3. Blast radius

Scope: account-wide. Every statement is Resource: *; nothing is scoped by bucket, role, region, or tag.
Confidentiality: all S3 data is readable now; via Path A, effectively all data the escalated role can reach.
Integrity: modify/delete any S3 object; run compute as privileged roles; create functions.
Availability: delete S3 data including S3-resident backups; RunInstances on * with no instance-type/region/count limits is the classic cryptomining and cost-bomb vector.
Lateral/cross-account: escalation to a privileged role can pivot to full account compromise, and onward through any cross-account trust the escalated role holds.

Net: a single compromise of this service account credential is plausibly equivalent to compromise of the whole account.
4. Remediation priorities
P0 — Constrain iam:PassRole. This is the highest-leverage single change because it severs the escalation keystone before you even touch the compute actions. Two dimensions, do both:

Scope Resource to the specific role ARNs this account legitimately passes.
Add Condition with iam:PassedToService limited to the service(s) actually needed (ec2.amazonaws.com and/or lambda.amazonaws.com).

P0 — Scope s3:* down. Always-live, account-wide data exfil/tamper/destroy. Depending on what your account holds (esp. if CloudTrail/config/state buckets are in scope) this is co-equal with PassRole. Replace * action with the specific actions on specific buckets.
P1 — Add conditions to ec2:RunInstances and lambda:CreateFunction. Even after PassRole is scoped, constrain instance types, regions, AMIs, and require tags/VPC; for Lambda, pin the execution role and require VPC config.
P2 — Remove anything genuinely unused, then add a permission boundary on any role this principal can pass or create, so even a successful create caps effective permissions.
The ordering logic: PassRole first because it's the difference between "can read S3" and "can become admin"; S3 right alongside it because it needs no escalation to be catastrophic; compute conditions next as defense-in-depth.
5. Least-privilege replacement strategy
Don't hand-guess the final policy — derive it. The reliable method:

Run IAM Access Analyzer policy generation, which builds a candidate policy from this principal's actual CloudTrail history. That tells you what it really uses versus what it's been granted.
Replace s3:* with concrete actions, splitting bucket-level (arn:aws:s3:::bucket) from object-level (arn:aws:s3:::bucket/*) resources.
Replace iam:PassRole on * with explicit role ARNs plus the iam:PassedToService guard.
Condition the compute actions.
Back it with a permission boundary on passable/creatable roles, and ideally an org SCP that globally denies the dangerous shapes (e.g., deny passing admin-tagged roles, deny RunInstances without required tags, deny making the trail bucket public). SCPs catch this class of mistake account-wide regardless of identity policy drift.

  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "S3ScopedAccess",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-app-data-bucket/*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "S3ListSpecificBucket",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:ListBucket"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-app-data-bucket"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "PassOnlyWorkloadRoleToEC2",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["iam:PassRole"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/my-app-ec2-runtime-role",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": { "iam:PassedToService": "ec2.amazonaws.com" }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "RunInstancesConstrained",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["ec2:RunInstances"],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "aws:RequestedRegion": "us-east-1",
          "aws:RequestTag/owner": "my-app"
        },
        "StringLike": { "ec2:InstanceType": ["t3.*", "m6i.large"] }
      }
    }
  ]
}
Notes on the template: I dropped lambda:CreateFunction and the second PassedToService value entirely — add them back only if the service genuinely creates Lambdas, and if so, pin a dedicated Lambda execution role ARN with iam:PassedToService = lambda.amazonaws.com. The RunInstances resource stays * because it spans many sub-resources (subnets, AMIs, ENIs); you tighten it with conditions and by scoping which AMIs/subnets are allowed rather than via the resource string. Tune the tag/region/instance-type conditions to your environment.
If it's useful I can turn this into a downloadable file with both the original and remediated policies side by side, plus an SCP example.
6. Detections
Map each capability to a CloudTrail signal and back it with managed detections.
PassRole — there's a common misconception you can just filter eventName = PassRole; in practice you detect it at the point of use. Inspect the request parameters of the consuming calls: RunInstances carries iamInstanceProfile, CreateFunction carries role. Alert when:

this principal passes a role it has never passed before, or
any principal passes a role tagged privileged/admin to EC2 or Lambda.

EC2 / the Path A escalation — the cleanest catch for the actual attack is GuardDuty's instance-credential-exfiltration findings (role credentials minted for an EC2 instance being used from an IP outside that instance / outside AWS). That fires precisely when the attacker takes the role creds off the box and uses them elsewhere. Also alert on RunInstances with an instance profile more privileged than the launcher, unusual instance types (GPU/large → mining), unusual regions/AMIs, or high counts; and on GuardDuty crypto-mining findings.

Back with GuardDuty S3 protection findings and Macie for sensitive-data discovery.
Defense-evasion tripwires — high-severity alerts on StopLogging, DeleteTrail, and PutBucketPolicy against the trail bucket; GuardDuty's CloudTrail-logging-disabled finding.
Foundation — make sure a multi-region org CloudTrail is on, enable GuardDuty with the EC2/S3/Lambda protection plans, run IAM Access Analyzer (external-access and unused-access), and correlate in Security Hub / Detective. Add an impossible-travel / new-ASN alert on this service account's credential specifically, since that's your earliest signal the key has leaked.

These four permissions are dangerous because each one, in different ways, lets a principal either run code as a more privileged identity, reach data broadly, or modify the things other privileged automation depends on. Before the five sections, here's the quick why for each:

iam:PassRole is the permission to hand an IAM role to an AWS service. On its own it does nothing, but paired with a service that executes code, it lets you attach a more privileged role to a resource you control. It's the single most important escalation primitive in AWS, and it's especially dangerous when scoped as Resource: * (pass any role, including admin).
Broad s3:* grants every S3 action, including modifying bucket policies/ACLs (make data public or cross-account-readable), deleting buckets, and writing objects. Write access to the wrong bucket — Lambda deployment zips, CloudFormation templates, CI artifacts, Terraform state — turns into code/config injection later.
ec2:RunInstances launches compute. An instance can carry an instance profile (a role); credentials for that role are retrievable from the instance metadata service, so launching an instance with a privileged profile yields that role's credentials.
lambda:CreateFunction lets you create and run arbitrary code under whatever execution role you specify — which means it's an escalation path as soon as it's combined with the ability to pass a privileged role and invoke the function.

1. How security teams assess blast radius
Blast radius is the total scope of damage if a given credential or identity is compromised. The key insight is that it is not just the permissions directly attached to an identity — it's the transitive closure over every escalation step that identity can take.
Teams typically (a) resolve effective permissions by combining identity-based policies, resource-based policies, SCPs, permission boundaries, and session policies into what the principal can actually do; (b) map transitive paths, modeling escalation edges as a graph ("this role can PassRole + CreateFunction, therefore it can become that role, which can reach admin"); (c) identify reachable resources and data, especially crown-jewel data stores, secrets, and other accounts via trust relationships; and (d) weigh exposure — an identity on a public-facing service, a CI/CD runner, or a developer laptop is a more likely entry point than a tightly held internal role.
Tooling that supports this includes IAM Access Analyzer, the IAM policy simulator, Cloudsplaining, PMapper (Principal Mapper, which produces "who can reach admin" graphs), Prowler, and ScoutSuite. The output you want is a prioritized list of identities ranked by how close they sit to admin or to sensitive data.
2. Why these permissions enable privilege escalation
The underlying mechanism: many AWS services perform actions as a role — an EC2 instance profile, a Lambda execution role, an ECS task role. If a lower-privileged principal can both influence which role gets attached and trigger execution, it inherits the higher role's permissions. iam:PassRole is the bridge that authorizes that delegation, which is why the dangerous patterns are pairings rather than single permissions:

PassRole + RunInstances → launch an instance carrying a privileged profile, then read that role's credentials from instance metadata.
PassRole + CreateFunction + InvokeFunction → execute arbitrary code under a privileged execution role.
PassRole + many other services (Glue, SageMaker, ECS, CloudFormation, Data Pipeline) — all accept a role and run something.

Broad s3:* is an escalation pivot in a different way: if it grants write access to a bucket holding executable artifacts (Lambda packages, CFN/Terraform templates, CI config), an attacker modifies what privileged automation later runs rather than escalating directly. There's also a family of pure-IAM self-escalation actions independent of PassRole — iam:CreatePolicyVersion, iam:AttachUserPolicy, iam:PutUserPolicy, iam:CreateAccessKey (for another user), iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy, iam:AddUserToGroup — that Rhino Security Labs documented as roughly two dozen distinct paths. The common thread is wildcard scoping: PassRole with Resource: *, or s3:* across all buckets, removes the boundary that would otherwise contain the action.
3. What least-privilege design looks like
The goal is to scope tightly and to ensure no single identity holds both halves of an escalation pair.
Scope resources rather than using * — PassRole should name exact role ARNs that are safe to pass; S3 actions should target specific buckets and prefixes. Constrain with condition keys: iam:PassedToService limits which service a role can be passed to; aws:SourceArn/aws:SourceAccount mitigate confused-deputy problems; aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent, region conditions, and tag-based (ABAC) conditions narrow further. Split read, write, and admin into separate policies, and avoid action wildcards (s3:*, iam:*) by enumerating the actions actually needed — Access Analyzer can generate a policy from observed CloudTrail usage so you right-size from real behavior.
Layer in guardrails that hold even if someone over-grants: permission boundaries cap the maximum permissions an identity can ever have (essential when delegating IAM-creation rights), and SCPs at the org level can deny dangerous actions, lock regions, and prevent anyone from disabling logging. Prefer short-lived credentials via STS or IAM Identity Center over long-lived access keys, and favor just-in-time elevation over standing admin. Finally, run regular access reviews and remove unused permissions using Access Analyzer's unused-access findings and IAM last-accessed data.
4. What logs defenders should monitor
CloudTrail is the primary source; the highest-signal events are:

IAM mutations: CreateAccessKey, AttachUserPolicy/AttachRolePolicy, PutUserPolicy/PutRolePolicy, CreatePolicyVersion, UpdateAssumeRolePolicy, CreateUser, CreateLoginProfile/UpdateLoginProfile, AddUserToGroup.
PassRole in context: it surfaces inside other events — watch RunInstances, CreateFunction, UpdateFunctionCode, and AssociateIamInstanceProfile, and check which role is being passed; correlate a pass with subsequent use of that role.
Lambda: CreateFunction, UpdateFunctionCode, AddPermission (resource-policy changes), and Invoke as a data event.
S3: PutBucketPolicy, PutBucketAcl, and especially PutBucketPublicAccessBlock (someone disabling the public-access block), DeleteBucket, plus selective S3 data events (GetObject/PutObject/DeleteObject) on sensitive buckets — these are high-volume, so enable them targeted rather than everywhere.
GuardDuty findings: UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration (instance-role credentials used from outside EC2 — a strong exfil signal), the PrivilegeEscalation and Recon:IAMUser finding families, and anomalous API calls from new geolocations or ASNs.
Logging tampering: alert on anyone touching the telemetry pipeline — StopLogging, DeleteTrail, PutEventSelectors (reducing coverage), DeleteFlowLogs, or disabling the KMS keys behind your logs.

Deliver CloudTrail to a centralized, object-lock (write-once) bucket in a separate logging account and forward to a SIEM, and pair it with AWS Config for configuration drift.
5. How to prioritise remediation
Order the work by risk, roughly:
First, stop active or exposed bleeding — rotate any leaked or unrotated long-lived keys and close internet-reachable admin paths. Second, break self-contained escalation pairs: any single identity holding both a broadly scoped PassRole and a compute-create action (RunInstances, CreateFunction) is top priority, as is any wildcard admin grant (iam:*, *:*, PassRole on Resource: *). Third, reduce cross-account and public exposure — resource or trust policies that name * as principal or allow untrusted accounts. Fourth, prune unused dangerous permissions, which IAM last-accessed data makes easy to find and low-risk to remove. Fifth, do the systematic right-sizing toward least privilege, installing permission boundaries and SCPs as durable guardrails so the gains don't erode.
A useful heuristic for ranking individual findings is reachability × likelihood: how close the path gets to admin or crown-jewel data, multiplied by how exposed the identity is (internet-facing, CI/CD, third-party, long-lived keys). Quick, high-impact wins — enabling S3 Public Access Block, adding an SCP, scoping one PassRole resource — should be done immediately even while the larger refactors are scheduled.
If it's useful, I can sketch the escalation-path graph for a specific set of roles, or help translate any of this into concrete policy JSON, SCP guardrails, or detection rules for your SIEM.

This is a textbook horizontal scan signature, and the single most important fact in your sample is the topology: a host on a user/workstation subnet (10.10.24.x) reaching out to a server subnet (10.10.1.x) on remote-access and lateral-movement ports (22/445/3389), at 02:00, fanning out to hundreds of hosts. That combination shifts the priors hard away from "sanctioned scanning." Here's how I'd work it.
1. Classification: which of the three is it?
You can't confirm from the sample alone, but you can rank the hypotheses and then pull the few fields that disambiguate.
What the current evidence suggests:

Legitimate admin/vuln scanning — unlikely. Vuln scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Rapid7) run from dedicated appliances on a management segment, not a user workstation, and they're typically allowlisted and scheduled. A vuln scan also tends to hit many ports per host (full TCP sweeps), whereas your sample shows a small curated port set. If 10.10.24.55 is a known scanner or has a scanning service account, this flips — so verify the asset's identity first.
Worm / malware self-propagation — plausible. Self-spreading malware originates from an infected endpoint (a workstation fits), targets a fixed, small port set tied to known exploits/abuse (445 SMB, 3389 RDP, 22 SSH are the classic lateral trio), and often enumerates IPs sequentially with near-identical timing. The off-hours start, when the user is away and automation runs unobserved, fits this too.
Hands-on / C2-driven recon — plausible. Post-compromise tooling (nmap, masscan, CrackMapExec/NetExec, Impacket) produces the same horizontal fan-out but is usually "lumpier": pauses and resumes, a wider or more deliberate port selection, and follow-up auth or exploit traffic against the hosts that allowed the connection.

The discriminators that will settle it:

Port cardinality. Pull count(distinct dport) for this source. ~3–5 fixed ports → worm/tooling lateral set. Dozens/hundreds of ports per host → vuln-style sweep.
TCP flags / flow completion. SYN-only with no handshake completion = pure discovery scan. Completed handshakes followed by data = something is actually connecting, which raises the severity.
What happened on the allowed hops. Did any allowed 445/3389/22 connection turn into an authentication event? That's the line between "noisy scan" and "active lateral movement."
Source-port pattern. masscan/zmap leave fixed or patterned source ports; nmap and worms look different. Useful for tool attribution.

My leaning on what you've shown: most consistent with worm propagation or post-compromise reconnaissance, least consistent with sanctioned scanning — but confirm via the asset identity and the four discriminators above before you commit.
2. Useful log fields and enrichment
Beyond the five fields in your sample, the high-value flow/firewall fields are protocol and TCP flags (SYN-only vs. completed), bytes and packets per flow (scans are tiny — a few packets, near-zero bytes; real sessions carry data), flow duration, source port, connection state/disposition (RST / timeout / established), TTL (OS fingerprint / spoof check), and the NAT/zone/interface context.
Enrichment that turns the flow record into a verdict:

Asset context for 10.10.24.55 — owner, role, OS, and crucially is it a sanctioned scanner? Plus a behavioral baseline: does this host normally talk to the server subnet at all?
Identity — which user/account was logged in during the window (correlate to AD auth: Windows 4624/4625, Kerberos TGT issuance).
DNS/DHCP — hostname and lease history for the IP.
Host/EDR telemetry — the process behind the connections (PID → path, hash, signer, parent, command line). This is the bridge to question 4.
Patch/vuln status of both the source and the targeted servers (which exploitable services were exposed on the allowed hops).
Auth outcomes on destinations — did any allowed SMB/RDP/SSH connection result in a successful logon? Correlate firewall allowed events with destination security logs.

3. Detection thresholds
Build three distinct detections; a single threshold blurs different behaviors. Treat the numbers below as starting points to baseline against your environment — percentile baselining per peer group (flag sources above the ~99th percentile of distinct-destination count for their subnet role) generalizes far better than fixed counts, and you must allowlist known scanners, vuln-management, SCCM/config-push, backup, and monitoring systems or you'll drown in false positives.

Horizontal scan (one port, many hosts): a single internal source contacting ≥25 distinct internal destinations on the same port within 60s, or ≥100 distinct within 5 min.
Vertical scan / port sweep (one host, many ports): a single source hitting ≥15 distinct ports on a single destination within 60s.
Block-heavy fan-out: ≥50 blocked attempts to ≥20 distinct destinations in 5 min — high-fidelity for blind scanning into segmented space.
Velocity / new-pair: connection rate exceeding the source's own baseline, weighted by the count of never-before-seen src→dst pairs.

Tier severity by destination sensitivity — the same fan-out aimed at the server subnet should outrank workstation-to-workstation noise. Your event would have tripped both the horizontal and block-heavy rules.
4. Finding the source process
The fast path is EDR: pivot on source IP + the 02:00–02:15 window to the owning PID, then read process path, file hash, code signer, parent process, command line, and start time. Parent process and command line usually tell you immediately whether it's nmap.exe, a script interpreter, a service, or unsigned malware.
Without EDR, on Windows during the window: Sysmon Event ID 3 (network-connect, tied to process) is ideal historically; live, use netstat -anob or Get-NetTCPConnection -State SynSent joined to Get-Process by PID, or Sysinternals TCPView/Process Monitor. Then check persistence: scheduled tasks, services, Run keys, WMI event subscriptions, and recently created executables (Prefetch, Amcache, ShimCache) to find how it got there. On Linux: ss -tnp / lsof -i, /proc/<pid>, and auditd.
Sequence it right for forensics: capture volatile state — memory, then the process binary's hash — before you reboot or reimage. Correlating the flow timestamps to process-start time narrows the candidate set quickly.
5. Containment
Move fast because the activity is active, but don't destroy evidence in the process:

Isolate the host. EDR network containment is preferred — it stops spread while preserving your investigative channel. Otherwise quarantine VLAN / restrictive ACL / disable the switch port.
Block at the firewall — deny 10.10.24.55 to the server subnet pending investigation, as a backstop to host isolation.
Preserve evidence — memory image and disk acquisition before remediation.
Contain credentials — if a user/service account was involved and any auth to destinations succeeded, disable/reset it (priority on privileged accounts) and revoke Kerberos tickets. Reserve heavier measures (e.g., krbtgt resets) for confirmed domain compromise.
Scope the blast radius — for every destination that allowed a connection, triage that host for secondary compromise, focusing on ones with a successful logon.
Hunt for patient-zero vs. spread — confirm whether 10.10.24.55 is the only source or whether the same fan-out pattern appears from other hosts.

6. Hardening
The structural fix is that a user workstation should never have had open lateral paths to server admin ports in the first place:

East-west segmentation / microsegmentation — default-deny workstation-to-server on 22/445/3389; restrict those protocols to jump hosts / Privileged Access Workstations. Enforce with VLAN ACLs and host-based firewall, plus NAC/802.1x to govern what connects.
Constrain lateral movement — disable SMBv1, enforce SMB signing, deploy LAPS so local admin passwords aren't reusable, restrict RDP logon rights to admins with Network Level Authentication, adopt a tiered admin model.
Visibility — deploy the question-3 detections on east-west traffic, EDR everywhere with tamper protection, and Sysmon with a network/process-aware config.
Reduce exploitable surface — patch management focused on the worm-relevant classes (MS17-010-style SMB, RDP/BlueKeep), least privilege, MFA on remote access, and disabling unused services on servers.
High-fidelity tripwires — canary/honeypot hosts on the server subnet that nothing legitimate should ever contact; a single connection to one becomes an instant, near-zero-false-positive alert.

If it's useful, I can turn this into a structured IR runbook or a one-page triage checklist for this specific scenario, or sketch the SIEM/Sigma correlation logic for the three detections in question 3 — just say which.

response_text:
Network scanning is one of the most common things a SOC sees, and most of it is benign. The core challenge isn't detecting scans — it's separating authorized asset discovery, monitoring, and vulnerability scanning from genuine adversary reconnaissance. Almost everything below ultimately serves that discrimination problem, so it's worth stating the discriminators up front: provenance (is the source a known, authorized asset?), regularity (legit scanners are scheduled and bounded; attackers explore), technique (standard connect scans vs evasion), and outcome chaining (does the scan lead to exploitation or lateral movement?).
1. Common scan patterns
The two foundational shapes:

Horizontal scan (network sweep): one source → many destination IPs on the same port(s). "Where does SMB/SSH/RDP live on this network?" In telemetry this is high destination-IP diversity, low port diversity.
Vertical scan (port scan): one source → one destination IP → many ports. "What's running on this box?" High port diversity, single destination.
Block scan: the combination — many hosts × many ports.

At the packet level, the technique matters because it changes the telemetry signature:

SYN ("half-open") scan: SYN sent, SYN-ACK or RST received, then RST without completing the handshake. Produces many short, asymmetric flows with tiny byte counts and lots of unestablished connections.
Connect scan: full three-way handshake then immediate teardown. Looks more like legitimate traffic, but appears in high volume with near-zero data transfer.
ACK scan: used to map firewall rules (stateful vs stateless), inferred from RST responses.
FIN / NULL / Xmas scans: unusual flag combinations (FIN-only, no flags, FIN+PSH+URG) to evade naive filters. These are high-signal because legitimate traffic almost never uses these combinations.
UDP scan: datagrams that elicit ICMP type 3 code 3 (port unreachable) from closed ports; slow and ICMP-noisy.
Idle/zombie scan: uses a third party's IP ID sequence to obscure the true source.

Evasion characteristics layered on top: low-and-slow timing (spread over hours/days to stay under thresholds), randomized destination order, decoy sources, packet fragmentation, and source-port spoofing (e.g., source port 53 or 80 to masquerade as DNS/HTTP). Preceding all of this you'll often see host-discovery: ICMP echo sweeps, ARP scans on the local segment, or TCP SYN/ACK probes to common ports.
2. Useful log fields
Primary sources are firewall logs, NetFlow/IPFIX, Zeek, IDS (Suricata/Snort), NDR, EDR, and DNS logs. The fields that do the heavy lifting:

Timestamp, plus flow start/end and duration
Source IP, source port; destination IP, destination port
Protocol (TCP/UDP/ICMP)
TCP flags (SYN/ACK/FIN/RST/PSH/URG) — essential for distinguishing scan techniques
Bytes and packets in each direction — scans are tiny and frequently asymmetric
Connection/flow state — in Zeek's conn.log, conn_state values like S0 (SYN seen, no reply), REJ (rejected), or RSTOS0 are strong signals when they appear en masse from one source; history encodes the flag sequence
ICMP type/code (type 8 echo request; type 3 code 3 unreachable)
Firewall action (allow/deny/drop)
TTL / IP ID anomalies (crafted packets, idle scans)
Interface / VLAN / zone
Derived aggregates: distinct destination IPs and distinct destination ports per source per window
Enrichment: source ASN/geo/reputation, and asset/user identity from CMDB, NAC, DHCP, or AD

The single most useful derived metric is fan-out — unique destinations (IPs or ports) a source touches in a time window — combined with the ratio of failed to successful connections.
3. Thresholding approaches

Fan-out counting: flag a source exceeding X unique destination IPs on a given port within Y seconds (horizontal), or X unique ports on one host (vertical).
Failed-connection ratio: a high proportion of SYN-only, RST, rejected, or ICMP-unreachable responses relative to established connections. Benign hosts mostly connect successfully; scanners mostly fail.
Sequential hypothesis testing (Threshold Random Walk): rather than a fixed count, treat each new-destination connection as evidence and accumulate likelihood that the source is a scanner based on success/failure outcomes. This is the classic Jung et al. approach and underlies several IDS implementations — it catches scanners faster and with fewer false positives than raw counting.
Tool-specific: Snort's sfPortscan tracks negative responses per source with low/medium/high sensitivity; Suricata supports rate_filter/thresholding and flow tracking; Zeek ships scan-detection notices.
Window design: fixed windows are cheap but miss low-and-slow; sliding windows catch slow scans at higher state cost. A common pattern is to run both — a short, sensitive window for noisy scans and a long window (hours) for low-and-slow.
Aggregation key: per-source-IP is the default, but NAT collapses many users behind one IP, so you may need per-source-port or per-identity aggregation to avoid both misses and false positives.

The tuning tension is straightforward: set thresholds too low and vulnerability scanners and monitoring tools bury you in alerts; too high and you miss deliberate slow scans.
4. False positives
A large share of "scan" alerts are authorized activity. The usual suspects:

Vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Rapid7, OpenVAS) — these are scanners by design.
Asset discovery / inventory (Lansweeper, SCCM, Tanium, IT-run Nmap).
Availability monitoring (Nagios, Zabbix, SolarWinds, PRTG) polling many hosts on fixed ports continuously.
Load balancer and service-mesh health checks probing backend pools.
Misbehaving applications — connection-pool storms, aggressive retry/failover logic hitting many hosts.
Local-segment discovery — mDNS, SSDP, ARP, printer/conferencing discovery.
Cloud auto-scaling and east-west service traffic.
Internet background radiation hitting the perimeter — almost always external and blocked, but constant.

The discriminators that resolve most of these: Is the source a known, authorized asset? Is there a corresponding change ticket or scheduled scan window? Does the activity recur on a regular, cron-like cadence (a hallmark of monitoring and scheduled scans)? Does it stay within an expected, bounded set of ports and hosts? Authorized scanning tends to be systematic and repetitive over the same scope; adversary recon tends to be exploratory, irregular, and curious about sensitive assets or unusual ports.
5. Detection strategies

Allowlist known scanners first. This is effectively step zero — suppressing authorized vuln scanners and monitoring hosts is what makes everything else readable.
Signature/threshold rules in IDS plus SIEM correlation counting fan-out and failed ratios.
Flow-based behavioral analytics on NetFlow — scales to large environments without full packet capture.
Baselining / UEBA / NDR — learn each host's normal connection footprint and flag deviations (sudden high destination diversity, port entropy spikes, new source talking to many internal hosts it never touched).
Deception — a network telescope (unused/darknet IP space) or internal honeypots produce extremely high-fidelity signal, because nothing legitimate should ever connect to them. Any touch is suspicious by definition.
Threat-intel enrichment on external sources, with the caveat that some scanners (Shodan, Censys) are benign-ish research traffic.
Signal combination. A single threshold trip is weak. Confidence comes from stacking indicators: high fan-out and high failed ratio and unusual TCP flags and a first-seen source and off-hours timing.
Map detections to MITRE ATT&CK: T1046 (Network Service Discovery), T1018 (Remote System Discovery), and T1595 (Active Scanning, external). Aligning rules to these techniques helps with coverage gaps.

6. Investigation steps
When a scan alert fires:

Identify the source. Internal or external? Resolve to an asset, owner, and identity via DHCP, DNS, NAC, AD, or CMDB. Is it already a known scanner?
Characterize the scan. Horizontal or vertical? Which ports and hosts, how fast, and what technique (SYN/connect/UDP/flag-based)? Pull the underlying flows or conn.log entries.
Check authorization. Look for a change ticket, a scheduled scan window, or membership in your approved-scanner allowlist. Confirm with IT or the asset owner.
Assess success, not just attempts. Did any connections actually establish (SYN-ACK, resp_bytes > 0, established state)? Reconnaissance attempts against a hardened network are far less urgent than successful enumeration.
Hunt for follow-on activity — this is the decisive question. After scanning, did the source attempt authentication, exploitation, or lateral movement, or connect back to the open ports it found? Pivot on the source across auth logs, EDR, and proxy data. Recon that chains into action is the real incident.
Pivot on destinations. Were crown-jewel assets (domain controllers, databases) targeted, and did any respond?
Enrich the source. External: geo, ASN, reputation, known scanning service. Internal: is the host possibly compromised? Check EDR for unusual processes and recent alerts.
Build a timeline. Start time, ongoing vs one-off, periodic cadence.
Decide on containment. Compromised internal host → isolate and trigger IR. Noisy external source → verify the perimeter is blocking and consider a block.
Document and tune. False positive → allowlist the authorized scanner and refine the rule. True positive → escalate to incident response.

The thread running through all of it: legitimate asset discovery is attributable, scheduled, bounded, and uses standard techniques; suspicious reconnaissance is unattributed or anomalous, irregular, drawn to sensitive targets, and frequently uses evasion — and it's the recon that leads somewhere (auth attempts, exploitation, lateral movement) that turns a low-priority alert into an active investigation.

The unifying goal is to eliminate direct internet exposure of management and data ports. In rough order of preference:
The strongest target is identity-aware / Zero Trust access (Cloudflare Access, Tailscale, Teleport, AWS SSM Session Manager, Azure Bastion, GCP IAP), where the user/device is authenticated before any network path opens — there's no listening public port at all. response_text:
Exposing management ports to 0.0.0.0/0 (every IPv4 address on the internet) is one of the most common and most consequential cloud and network misconfigurations. The core problem is that these ports are gateways to privileged control, and once they face the open internet the only thing standing between an attacker and full compromise is authentication on a single service. Here's how that breaks down across the five areas you asked about.
1. How exposed services are commonly discovered
Exposure is discovered automatically and continuously, not just when someone decides to target you. The entire IPv4 space is scanned constantly:

Internet-wide indexing services like Shodan, Censys, ZoomEye, and BinaryEdge continuously scan all reachable addresses and index open ports plus service banners. A newly exposed service typically shows up in these databases within hours, fully searchable by anyone.
Mass scanners such as masscan and ZMap can sweep the entire internet for a single port in minutes. Attackers run these to build fresh target lists, then follow up with nmap for detailed fingerprinting.
Banner grabbing reveals software and version (OpenSSH x.y, a specific RDP build, MySQL/PostgreSQL/MongoDB versions), which is matched against CVE databases to identify exploitable hosts.
Passive reconnaissance — certificate transparency logs, DNS enumeration, and historical scan data — surfaces hostnames and IPs without ever touching your infrastructure.

The practical takeaway: "security through obscurity" does not work here. Nobody has to know you exist; the scanners find you because they scan everything. Time-to-discovery for an exposed port is effectively minutes to hours.
2. Why management ports are high risk
These ports are different from a public web server because they grant administrative or direct data access, so a single successful authentication usually equals full compromise rather than a limited foothold.
SSH (22) typically leads to a shell, often with root or sudo. RDP (3389) gives full interactive desktop and administrative control of a Windows host. Database ports — MySQL (3306), PostgreSQL (5432), MSSQL (1433), MongoDB (27017), Redis (6379), Elasticsearch (9200) — provide direct access to data, and several of these historically shipped with weak or no authentication by default, which is why so many "drive-by" database breaches and wipe-for-ransom incidents have occurred.
The risk concentrates for a few reasons. Authentication is the only control, with no network-layer defense in depth behind it, so credential attacks (brute force, password spraying, credential stuffing using leaked passwords) run around the clock from automated bots. RDP in particular is one of the most common ransomware entry vectors, and exposed databases are routinely found, copied, and held for ransom. On top of credential attacks, any unpatched pre-authentication vulnerability — BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) for RDP is the canonical example — turns mere exposure into immediate remote code execution. Finally, the blast radius is large: these are high-privilege interfaces, so compromise of one is frequently the launch point for lateral movement across the environment.
3. How defenders should prioritise remediation
Prioritisation should be risk-based rather than alphabetical, weighting the privilege of the service, the strength (or absence) of authentication, known exploitable CVEs, and whether the exposure is even necessary.
A reasonable triage order:

Unauthenticated or default-credential services on the internet — exposed databases, Redis, Elasticsearch, MongoDB, admin panels. These are compromised by automated drive-by attacks with no skill required. Fix immediately.
RDP exposed to the internet — extremely high ransomware risk even with authentication. Critical.
Services with known unpatched pre-auth RCEs — exposure plus a public exploit is a matter of time.
SSH with password authentication enabled — brute-forceable; should move to key-only.
Everything else exposed, ranked by data sensitivity and reachability.

In practice the workflow is inventory first, because you cannot remediate what you cannot see. Cloud-native tooling (AWS Config, Security Hub, GuardDuty; Azure Defender for Cloud; GCP Security Command Center) or a CSPM platform will enumerate every rule allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on sensitive ports. For each finding, validate whether the exposure is intentional, then either tighten the source range to known IPs or remove the rule entirely. The remediation itself is usually fast — a single firewall rule change — which is why the bottleneck is almost always discovery and ownership, not the fix. It's worth distinguishing findings with compensating controls (MFA, key-only auth, fully patched, behind a bastion) from those with none; the latter are far more urgent, though broad exposure remains a finding regardless because it enlarges attack surface and buries real intrusions in scan noise.
4. Safer access patterns
The goal is to remove management ports from the public internet entirely and default to deny. Several patterns achieve this, roughly in increasing order of robustness:

IP allowlisting restricts the source CIDR to known office or VPN egress addresses. Far better than 0.0.0.0/0, but brittle with dynamic IPs and still trusts anyone behind the allowed address.
Bastion / jump host funnels all management access through one hardened, heavily monitored entry point, shrinking the attack surface to a single auditable host.
VPN requires an authenticated tunnel before any internal management interface is reachable.
Identity-aware proxies and ZTNA — Cloudflare Access, Google IAP/BeyondCorp, Teleport, Tailscale, Azure Bastion. Access is brokered per-identity rather than per-network-location.
Agent-based access with zero inbound ports — AWS Systems Manager Session Manager is the strongest pattern here: the instance reaches out to the SSM service, so there are no open inbound management ports at all, and access is governed by IAM with full session logging. This eliminates the exposed-port problem entirely rather than guarding it.
Just-in-time access (Azure JIT VM access, PIM) opens a path only on approval, for a bounded time window.

Layer strong authentication on top regardless of pattern: SSH key-only with password auth disabled, MFA on RDP and VPN, certificate-based and short-lived credentials, and management-plane network segmentation away from the data plane. Databases specifically should never face the internet — reach them through private subnets, PrivateLink/VPC peering, or only via the application tier, always over TLS. Note that changing default ports or port-knocking is marginal; it lowers scan noise but is obscurity, not a control, and shouldn't be counted as remediation.
5. Monitoring recommendations
Effective monitoring catches both the misconfiguration and any attacks that follow.
For the misconfiguration itself, run continuous configuration and drift detection: alert on AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress events in CloudTrail (or the cloud equivalent) and use AWS Config rules / CSPM policies that fire the moment a rule is opened to 0.0.0.0/0 on a sensitive port, ideally blocking it at creation. Pair this with external attack-surface monitoring — periodically scanning your own public footprint, or subscribing to Shodan/ASM monitoring — so newly exposed services are caught independently of internal config.
For attacks, watch authentication logs for brute-force and spray patterns (high failed-login volume, logins from unusual geographies, impossible travel, off-hours admin logins, and especially a success following many failures). Use network telemetry (VPC Flow Logs, firewall logs) to spot connections to management ports from unexpected sources, and deploy IDS/IPS signatures for known exploits against these services. Cloud-native threat detection like GuardDuty surfaces SSH/RDP brute force and connections from known-bad infrastructure with little setup. For high-fidelity signal, honeypots or canary services are valuable: any interaction with a decoy management port is almost certainly malicious, with very low false positives. Centralise all of this in a SIEM so authentication, flow, and config events can be correlated rather than reviewed in isolation.
If it helps, I can turn any of these sections into a concrete checklist or a remediation runbook tailored to a specific cloud provider (AWS, Azure, or GCP).

IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) and BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization) describe the same flaw from two angles. BOLA is the term OWASP uses — it's #1 on the API Security Top 10 (API1:2023) — and IDOR is the older, more general name. The core problem: an endpoint exposes a reference to an object (a database ID, like /api/orders/1001) and authenticates the caller, but never verifies that this particular caller is allowed to access this particular object. So a logged-in User B changes the ID and reads User A's order.
The distinction that underpins everything below: authentication answers who are you (are you logged in?), while authorization answers what may you do. Authorization itself splits into function-level ("may you call this endpoint at all?") and object-level ("may you touch this specific instance?"). BOLA is specifically the failure of that last check. The endpoint may correctly require a valid session and even allow the "view orders" function in general — yet still fail to confirm that order 1001 belongs to the requester.
1. Checking authorization boundaries
You need at least two accounts you control, ideally at similar privilege levels for horizontal testing (A vs B) plus a low- and high-privilege pair for vertical testing. The basic procedure:
As User A, perform a legitimate action and capture the request and the object ID — say GET /api/orders/1001 returns A's order. Then, authenticated with User B's session token, replay the same request with A's ID. If B gets A's order back, that's the flaw.
Test this across every operation, not just reads:

GET — can you view another user's object?
PUT/PATCH — can you modify it?
DELETE — can you delete it?
POST — can you create objects referencing or on behalf of another user?

And probe the variations that catch real-world cases:

Enumeration — if IDs are sequential integers, can you just walk 1000, 1001, 1002…?
Every location the ID can live — path, query string, request body, headers, even a JWT claim. A handler may check one and trust the others.
Nested/indirect references — /api/orders/1001/items/5 needs checks on both the order and the item.
Parameter removal or tampering — sometimes omitting the ID returns all objects, or supplying a user_id in the body gets trusted.
UUIDs are not a fix — a non-sequential GUID only makes blind enumeration harder. If it leaks once (logs, referer headers, another endpoint, an email), the object is still reachable. That's obfuscation, not authorization.

Burp Suite extensions like Autorize or AuthMatrix automate the core comparison: you load User B's session into the tool, browse the app as User A, and the tool replays every request with B's credentials and flags any that succeed when they shouldn't.
2. Evidence that confirms the issue
The confirming evidence is a request authenticated as User B that successfully returns or modifies an object belonging exclusively to User A. Concretely:
A 2xx response containing A's actual data (A's name, address, order contents) in reply to a request carrying B's session — that's the smoking gun. The response should vary with the ID, not with who is asking: the same ID yields the same data regardless of which valid session sends it. For writes, the modification must actually persist — PATCH A's order as B, then verify out-of-band that the change took effect.
What does not confirm it, so you avoid false positives: a 403/401/404 is the correct, secure behavior (some apps deliberately return 404 rather than 403 to avoid confirming an object exists — that's fine). A 200 with empty or generic data isn't proof. And accessing your own object is obviously not a finding — which is exactly why you control both accounts: you know 1001 is A's because you created it as A. The clean proof is a small matrix: object owned by A + request made with B's token + response containing A's data, with both distinct sessions documented.
3. Why object-level authorization matters
It's the #1 API risk because it's both common and high-impact, and the reason it's common is instructive: the happy path works perfectly without the check. A user accessing their own data never triggers the missing logic, so the gap is invisible until someone deliberately tampers. The endpoint also looks secure — it demands a login — and developers conflate "must be authenticated" with "is authorized." But a logged-in attacker is still authenticated; authentication proves identity, not entitlement.
The impact is severe and usually scriptable. Because the flaw is often enumerable, a single BOLA can turn into wholesale exfiltration — loop through the IDs and dump every order, record, or piece of PII in the system — plus unauthorized modification, deletion, or privilege escalation.
Critically, it can't be fixed at the perimeter. A WAF, rate limiter, or auth gateway has no way to know whether order 1001 belongs to the requester; only the application holds that ownership relationship, so the decision must live in application logic, evaluated per-object and per-request. The principle to internalize: every request for a specific object must answer "does the currently authenticated principal have the right to perform this action on this object?" — and that answer must be derived server-side from the session, never from a client-supplied claim about identity.
4. Remediation
Enforce object-level authorization on every object-accessing request, deriving the user from the trusted session and checking against the requested object.
The most robust pattern is to scope the query to the authenticated user so unauthorized data simply can't be returned:
sqlSELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = :order_id AND user_id = :current_user_id
or in an ORM, Order.where(id: params[:id], user: current_user). If nothing comes back, return 404. This beats a separate ownership check because there's no "forgot to add the check" failure mode — the lookup itself can't yield another user's object.
Where sharing rules are too complex for that (e.g. delegated access), load the object and check explicitly: if (order.userId !== currentUser.id && !currentUser.canAccess(order)) return 404;. Because that's easy to omit on a new endpoint, centralize it in a policy or guard layer rather than scattering ad-hoc if owner checks — Pundit/CanCanCan in Rails, Spring Security method authorization (@PreAuthorize), middleware, or a policy engine like OPA. A single enforcement point every object access flows through is what prevents inconsistency.
Two rules sit underneath all of this: never trust client-supplied identity — the user ID must come from the validated session or token, never a body parameter the attacker can change — and default-deny, so anything not explicitly granted is refused and new endpoints are locked down by default. As hardening on top (not as the fix), return 404 rather than 403 for inaccessible objects to avoid leaking their existence, and treat UUIDs as defense-in-depth only after real authorization is in place.
5. Testing that the fix works
Re-run the original tests and confirm they now fail from the attacker's side, while legitimate use still works:
Start with a regression of the proof of concept — the request where B read A's order 1001 now returns 403/404 with no leaked data — and re-run the full matrix across GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE. Then confirm the legitimate path is intact: A can still access A's own order (200), so you know you didn't over-correct. Script an enumeration pass as B across a range of IDs and verify it only ever returns B's own objects, never A's. Re-test every injection point — path, query, body, headers — since a fix in one handler can miss another, and cover edge cases like nonexistent, malformed, and deleted IDs so they're handled consistently (ideally indistinguishable 404s).
Two things make the verification durable. First, encode the check as a permanent regression test in CI — an integration test asserting "User B requests User A's resource → expect 403/404" — so the fix survives future changes to the endpoint. Second, verify the centralized policy actually applies to all object-accessing endpoints, not just the one you patched; the single most common failure is fixing one route and leaving its siblings exposed. A real fix is demonstrated by the absence of unauthorized access across the whole surface, the presence of authorized access, and a test that guards against regression.
This is standard defensive work, but the same techniques can access data that isn't yours, so run it only against systems you own or are explicitly authorized to test — a written scope or bug-bounty program's rules.

Whether the response body comes back to you (full-read SSRF) or not (blind SSRF) matters a lot for impact — note which one you have.
2. Impact assessment
Severity scales with what's reachable:

Localhost admin reachable — High. Admin panels frequently bind to localhost on the assumption nothing can reach them; SSRF defeats that.
Internal host reachable (10.0.0.5) — High. Enables internal port scanning, mapping, and hitting services that trust the app server's network position, bypassing perimeter firewalls.
Metadata reachable (169.254.169.254) — Critical, typically CVSS 9+. On AWS with IMDSv1 enabled, /latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/ returns temporary IAM credentials whose blast radius equals the instance role's permissions. This is the exact chain behind the 2019 Capital One breach (SSRF → IMDS → credential theft → S3 exfiltration).

Full-read SSRF (response reflected to the attacker) is worse than blind, but blind SSRF still allows internal scanning, state-changing requests, and metadata access if results surface anywhere.
3. Logs that would show the internal requests
Check, in roughly this order:

Application/HTTP-client logs — outbound request logging from whatever library does the fetch (requests, axios, HttpClient, etc.). Often this is not logged, which is itself a finding.
Forward/egress proxy access logs — if outbound traffic is proxied, the destination shows here.
VPC Flow Logs — connections to internal IPs. Important caveat: traffic to the link-local IMDS address (169.254.169.254) historically does not appear in VPC Flow Logs, so absence there doesn't rule out metadata access.
CloudTrail — won't show the IMDS read itself, but will show use of leaked credentials (API calls from an unexpected IP/role), which is your real detection signal for the metadata case.
The target's own logs — the admin/internal service access log showing a request sourced from the app server's IP.
Host-level telemetry — conntrack, eBPF/EDR network records on the app host.

If outbound requests aren't logged anywhere, adding egress request logging is part of the fix.
4. Whether cloud metadata could be exposed
Determine the provider and IMDS posture:

AWS — Is IMDSv2 enforced (HttpTokens: required)? IMDSv1 (token-less GET) is the dangerous version; SSRF can read it trivially. IMDSv2 requires a PUT with a custom header to obtain a token, plus a hop limit — SSRF generally can't issue the PUT or set headers, so enforcing IMDSv2 and setting the hop limit to 1 is a strong mitigation. Separately, scope the instance role to least privilege so leaked credentials are low-value.
GCP — metadata requires Metadata-Flavor: Google by default, so plain SSRF usually can't read it, but check for any legacy/unauthenticated endpoints.
Azure — IMDS requires the Metadata: true header and a specific path; similar reasoning.

Safe test: confirm whether a request to the metadata IP is refused at the app and/or network layer. If you confirm real exposure, treat any potentially exposed credentials as compromised and rotate them.
5. Application-level mitigations
An allowlist of permitted destination domains is the strongest control — only the hosts you actually import from. If a strict allowlist isn't feasible, the robust validation pattern is resolve → validate the numeric IP → pin the connection:
pythonimport ipaddress, socket

def is_blocked(ip_str):
    ip = ipaddress.ip_address(ip_str)
    return (ip.is_private or ip.is_loopback or ip.is_link_local
            or ip.is_reserved or ip.is_multicast or ip.is_unspecified
            or ip in ipaddress.ip_network("100.64.0.0/10")        # CGNAT
            or (ip.version == 6 and ip.ipv4_mapped and is_blocked(str(ip.ipv4_mapped))))

# 1. Enforce scheme (http/https only) and port (80/443) BEFORE anything else.
# 2. Resolve the host to ALL its IPs; reject if ANY is blocked.
# 3. Open the connection to that exact validated IP (pin it) so it can't
#    change between check and fetch (defeats DNS rebinding / TOCTOU).
Key points the validator must get right:

Check numeric IP ranges, not URL strings. Regex on the URL is bypassable via decimal (http://2130706433/), hex (http://0x7f000001), octal (http://017700000001), shortened (http://127.1), IPv6, IPv4-mapped IPv6 ([::ffff:169.254.169.254]), and URL-encoded forms — all of which collapse to a blocked IP only after resolution.
Block dangerous schemes — only allow http/https; reject file://, gopher:// (can forge arbitrary TCP payloads), dict://, ftp://.
Control redirects — either disable redirect-following or re-run the full validation on every Location header. An allowed host returning a 302 to an internal IP is a classic bypass.
Don't reflect raw upstream responses or errors back to the user — this limits full-read SSRF and metadata leakage.
Defense in depth — tight timeouts, response size caps, and verifying the fetched bytes are actually an image (content-type + magic bytes). Ideally run the fetcher with no ambient cloud credentials.

6. Network egress controls
Layer network controls underneath the app fix so a validation bug isn't game-over:

Default-deny egress on the app servers (security groups / firewall), allowlisting only required destinations.
Block the metadata IP at the network layer where the app doesn't need it, and enforce IMDSv2 with hop limit 1 so proxied/containerized requests can't reach it.
Route outbound fetches through an egress proxy that enforces destination allowlisting and logs every request — this centralizes both policy and the logging gap from #3.
Network segmentation — app servers shouldn't have routes to admin panels, databases, or management interfaces unless strictly required; put those on a separate management network/subnet.
Kubernetes — NetworkPolicies to restrict pod egress, deny pod access to the node's 169.254.169.254, and use IRSA / Workload Identity so pods don't depend on node IMDS at all.

7. Regression tests
Wire these into CI so a future change can't silently reintroduce the bug. Cover the validator with both negative and positive cases:

Localhost forms: localhost, 127.0.0.1, 0.0.0.0, ::1, 127.1, 2130706433, 0x7f000001, 017700000001.
Private ranges: 10.x, 172.16–31.x, 192.168.x.
Link-local / metadata: 169.254.169.254 and its decimal/hex/IPv6-mapped variants.
Schemes: assert file://, gopher://, dict://, ftp:// are rejected.
Redirect test: a mock server that 302s to an internal IP → fetch must be blocked.
DNS rebinding test: mock the resolver to return public-then-internal → connection pinning must prevent it.
Ports: reject anything outside your allowed set.
Positive cases: legitimate allowed image URLs still succeed, so you don't break the feature.
Integration test: point the live endpoint at an OOB canary and assert it's blocked when it should be.
